newsitem.title: SPAIN: U.S. confidence in Latam rebounds,reforms to stick.
newsitem.headline: U.S. confidence in Latam rebounds,reforms to stick.

text.p: U.S. investor confidence in Latin America is rebounding as experts believe market reforms will stick although individual setbacks are possible, a BankBoston survey published on Sunday showed.

Eighty percent of U.S. investors are more confident in Latin America than five years ago and 59 percent believe the region's market-oriented economic reforms will survive, according to the poll which was released at the Inter-American Development Bank's 38th annual meeting.

"U.S. business leaders believe the region's economic and political reforms are real and will last and that it's time to invest aggressively in the region," said Peter Allen, managing director of emerging markets research at BankBoston.

The survey was conducted by Wirthlin Worldwide between February 17 and 27 and was based on telephone interviews of 303 U.S. financial executives. The poll surveyed Fortune 1000 senior executives, global banking and investment executives.

When asked whether free-market reforms could be reversed in one or more countries within the next decade, 65 percent of those surveyed said it would be likely and 34 percent said it would be unlikely.

"Investors are confident that the region will embrace market reforms for the long term, but they are not ruling out the possibility of setbacks in one or a couple of countries," said Chris Smith, a BankBoston managing director.

Investors believe political corruption is the most significant problem facing Latin America, with 38 percent of those surveyed citing it as a concern. Economic stability, unequal distribution, lack of a technological infrastructure and democratic instability were also worries.

Despite this, U.S. investors are eager to take part in Latin American privatisations with 48 percent ready "as soon as possible." Another 28 percent would wait five years, while seven percent would wait longer and 12 percent would never invest.
Financial debt and equity investors prefer Mexico as a Latin American investment location, while Fortune 1000 companies have their eye on Brazil, the survey showed.

Of those surveyed, 49 percent believe a hemispheric free-trade zone will not be created by the year 2005, a deadline proposed by hemispheric leaders at the summit of the Americas two years ago, while 46 percent say the deadline will be met.
